title: NJ Driver's Manual – Chapter 5
subtitle: Defensive Driving & Special Conditions
note: Based on the 2025 NJ Driver's Manual, Chapter 5. Verify all answers against the current manual before your exam.

questions.q: Defensive driving is best defined as:
opts: Driving aggressively to avoid slow drivers
Adjusting your driving to obey every traffic law
Anticipating hazards and responding safely before problems develop
Always driving at or below the speed limit
questions.exp: Defensive driving means actively scanning the road, predicting the actions of others, and taking precautionary action to avoid crashes — not merely reacting to them.

questions.q: In adverse conditions such as rain, fog, or ice, your following distance should be:
opts: The same as in dry, clear conditions
Reduced so you can react to the vehicle ahead
At least doubled — 6 or more seconds instead of 3
One car length per 10 mph of speed
questions.exp: Double your following distance (6+ seconds) in wet, icy, or foggy conditions. Stopping distances increase dramatically, and visibility is reduced.

questions.q: Hydroplaning occurs when:
opts: Your engine overheats on a wet road
Your tires ride on a film of water and lose contact with the road surface
Your windshield wipers cannot clear rain fast enough
Water enters through a window seal
questions.exp: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road, causing the tires to lose traction. It can occur at speeds as low as 35 mph on wet roads.

questions.q: To recover from hydroplaning, you should:
opts: Apply the brakes firmly and steer to the shoulder
Swerve quickly to the side to find dry pavement
Ease off the gas gradually; do NOT brake or steer sharply until tires regain contact
Accelerate to spin the tires back into contact
questions.exp: Ease off the accelerator gently. Sudden braking or steering while hydroplaning can cause a spin. Allow the tires to slow naturally and regain road contact before steering.

questions.q: 'Black ice' is dangerous primarily because:
opts: It forms only on bridges and overpasses
It melts quickly and makes the road slippery
It is a thin, transparent layer of ice nearly invisible on the pavement surface
It is blacker than normal ice and harder to remove
questions.exp: Black ice appears as a wet-looking sheen on the pavement. Because it is nearly invisible, drivers often fail to slow down in time. It commonly forms in shaded areas, bridges, and overpasses.

questions.q: During a rear-wheel skid (fishtail), you should steer:
opts: Sharply away from the direction the rear is sliding
Straight ahead and brake hard
Into the direction the rear of the car is sliding (in the direction you want the front to go)
To the left regardless of which way the car is sliding
questions.exp: For a rear-wheel skid, steer gently toward the direction the rear is sliding (often called 'steering into the skid') while easing off the gas. This straightens the vehicle.

questions.q: In fog, you should use:
opts: High beams to illuminate the road further ahead
Hazard flashers to alert other drivers
Low beams (or fog lights if equipped)
No lights — they create dangerous glare in fog
questions.exp: Use low beams in fog. High beams reflect off water droplets in the fog and create a 'white wall' of glare that actually reduces your ability to see.

questions.q: When driving in heavy fog, you should:
opts: Speed up to get out of the fog faster
Follow another vehicle closely to use their lights as a guide
Reduce your speed significantly, use low beams, and increase your following distance
Turn on your high beams and keep your speed
questions.exp: In heavy fog, slow down well below the posted limit, use low beams (not high beams), increase following distance, and be prepared to stop for hazards you cannot see until the last moment.

questions.q: High beams must be dimmed to low beams when:
opts: You are within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle, or within 200–300 feet of a vehicle ahead
Only when the oncoming driver flashes their lights
Only in residential areas
Only between 10 PM and 6 AM
questions.exp: Dim your high beams when within 500 feet of oncoming traffic (approaching from the front) or within 200–300 feet when following another vehicle. High beams temporarily blind other drivers.

questions.q: 'Overdriving your headlights' means driving at a speed where:
opts: You are using high beams when low beams would suffice
You cannot stop within the distance illuminated by your headlights
Your headlights are too bright for the road
You are faster than your headlights can track
questions.exp: Overdriving your headlights means you are going so fast that your stopping distance exceeds how far your headlights let you see. If a hazard appears at the edge of your visibility, you cannot stop in time.

questions.q: If your brakes suddenly fail while driving, the recommended sequence of actions is:
opts: Immediately turn the ignition off
Shift into reverse to slow the vehicle
Pump the brake pedal rapidly (this may restore hydraulic pressure), downshift to a lower gear, and use the parking brake gradually
Swerve off the road at the first opportunity
questions.exp: Pump the brakes rapidly to try to restore hydraulic pressure. Downshift to slow the engine. Apply the parking/emergency brake gradually (not suddenly). Look for a safe escape route — a runaway-truck ramp, uphill slope, or soft shoulder.

questions.q: What is the biggest danger of 'highway hypnosis' (monotony)?
opts: High speed in curves
The driver becomes drowsy or inattentive due to the monotonous straight road and may stop scanning actively
Sun glare on straight highways
Wind buffeting on open roads
questions.exp: Long, featureless highways can lull drivers into a trance-like state where they lose awareness of their surroundings. To avoid it: keep eyes moving, take breaks every 2 hours, and make sure you are well rested.

questions.q: The most effective prevention for driver fatigue is:
opts: Drinking a caffeinated beverage every hour
Opening windows for fresh air
Getting adequate sleep before driving and taking a real rest break every 2 hours
Playing loud music to stay alert
questions.exp: Only genuine rest and sleep restores alertness. Caffeine, fresh air, and loud music provide only temporary, unreliable stimulation and should never be substituted for real rest.

questions.q: Stopping distances on ice or snow compared to dry pavement can be:
opts: About the same if you have good tires
Twice as long
3 to 12 times longer
Only slightly longer at low speeds
questions.exp: Ice and snow dramatically reduce tire-road friction. Stopping distances can be 3 to 12 times greater than on dry pavement, which is why much greater following distances are required.

questions.q: When your vehicle begins to skid, the very first action you should take is:
opts: Apply the brakes immediately
Ease off the gas (accelerator) gradually
Steer sharply in the opposite direction
Shift to neutral
questions.exp: Ease off the gas first. Sudden braking or sharp steering during a skid often makes it worse. Decelerating gradually allows you to regain some control before correcting your steering.

questions.q: The 'space cushion' in defensive driving means:
opts: The time delay before reacting to a hazard
Maintaining adequate open space around your vehicle in all directions at all times
The recommended gap between your vehicle and a truck
The distance needed to complete an emergency stop
questions.exp: A space cushion — open space maintained on all sides of your vehicle — gives you time and room to react and maneuver if another driver makes a mistake.

questions.q: When driving at night, you should drive at a speed where you can:
opts: Stop within twice the distance your headlights illuminate
Stop within the distance you can see with your headlights
Always stop within 300 feet
Keep pace with other traffic regardless of headlight range
questions.exp: Drive at a speed where you can stop within the distance your headlights illuminate. Driving faster means if a hazard appears at the edge of your headlight range, you cannot stop in time.

questions.q: After driving through a deep puddle or flooded section of road, you should:
opts: Accelerate to dry the brakes quickly with friction
Come to a complete stop on the road to inspect for damage
Gently tap and apply your brakes several times to dry them and restore normal braking
Do nothing — modern disc brakes are self-cleaning
questions.exp: Water can reduce braking effectiveness. After driving through deep water, gently tap the brakes a few times to build heat and dry the brake surfaces. Test your stopping ability before returning to normal speeds.

questions.q: Distracted driving includes all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Eating or drinking while driving
Adjusting the car stereo or navigation while moving
Daydreaming or being lost in thought
Checking mirrors every 5–8 seconds
questions.exp: Regularly checking mirrors is a safe, recommended practice — not a distraction. Distracted driving involves any activity that diverts attention from the primary task of driving: visual, manual, or cognitive.

questions.q: Road rage can most effectively be avoided by:
opts: Responding firmly to show other drivers you will not be intimidated
Slowing down or blocking an aggressive driver
Not engaging — allowing space, avoiding eye contact, and not responding to provocations
Honking back to establish your position
questions.exp: The safest response to an aggressive driver is to not engage. Give them space, avoid eye contact, and do not retaliate. If threatened, do not stop — drive to a police station or busy public area.

questions.q: In a work zone, drivers should:
opts: Maintain highway speed to reduce time in the zone
Follow the vehicle ahead closely to limit the number of vehicles in the zone
Slow down significantly, stay alert, and obey all signs and flagger instructions
Sound their horn to alert workers
questions.exp: Work zones are among the most dangerous places on the road. Reduce speed, increase following distance, eliminate distractions, and always obey flaggers and signs.

questions.q: To avoid 'target fixation' (driving toward what you're looking at), you should:
opts: Focus intently on the center of the lane ahead
Stare at the hazard to judge how to react
Look where you WANT to go, not at the hazard
Close your eyes briefly to reset your focus
questions.exp: Target fixation causes drivers to steer toward whatever they are staring at. Look beyond and around hazards — toward where you want to go — and your hands will naturally follow your eyes.

questions.q: When a tire blows out at highway speed, the correct first response is to:
opts: Apply the brakes hard immediately
Grip the wheel firmly, ease off the gas (do NOT brake suddenly), and steer straight
Swerve immediately to the shoulder
Shift into neutral and coast to a stop
questions.exp: A blowout often causes a strong pull to one side. Grip the wheel firmly, resist the pull, ease off the gas, and let the vehicle slow naturally before gently steering to the shoulder.

questions.q: Sun glare while driving can best be managed by:
opts: Wearing regular sunglasses and maintaining speed
Closing your eyes briefly to protect your vision
Using the sun visor, wearing polarized sunglasses, and slowing down; if blinded, look to the right edge of the road
Using high beams to illuminate the road ahead despite the glare
questions.exp: Use the visor and sunglasses to reduce glare. If momentarily blinded, slow down and look toward the right edge of the road (painted fog line) to maintain your lane position.

questions.q: On a curve, the safest technique is to:
opts: Accelerate through the curve to reduce time in it
Brake firmly in the middle of the curve if needed
Slow down before entering the curve, then gently accelerate through it
Maintain exactly the posted speed limit
questions.exp: Enter curves at a safe, reduced speed. Braking mid-curve can cause a skid. Gently accelerating through a curve improves stability by transferring weight toward the rear wheels.

questions.q: Which of the following is the safest response to an approaching aggressive driver who is tailgating you?
opts: Brake-check the tailgater to force them to back off
Speed up so they cannot keep up
Gradually slow down to create more space ahead, making it easier for the tailgater to pass
Pull over immediately and stop
questions.exp: Create more space ahead of you so you can brake gradually if needed. Signal and move right when safe, allowing the aggressive driver to pass. Brake-checking can cause a rear-end crash.

questions.q: When your engine stalls while driving at speed, you should:
opts: Immediately apply the parking brake
Steer calmly toward a safe area while you still have momentum and power-assisted steering, signal, and coast to a stop
Shift to reverse to restart the engine
Turn the ignition off and on rapidly to restart while rolling
questions.exp: Power steering and power brakes still work for a short time after stall. Steer safely to the shoulder while the vehicle still moves. Use the ignition switch to restart — but don't try this at high speed.

questions.q: When following a large truck, the greatest danger is:
opts: The truck's exhaust affecting your engine
Being in the truck's blind spot — the driver cannot see you and may change lanes or brake unexpectedly
Losing control in the truck's wind wake
Road debris from the truck's tires
questions.exp: Large trucks have extensive blind spots. If you cannot see the truck driver in their mirrors, they cannot see you. Increase following distance so you can see their mirrors and they can see your vehicle.

questions.q: What is the 'No Zone' around large trucks?
opts: The distance where a truck must stop by law
The areas directly in front, behind, and on both sides where the truck driver has little or no visibility
The speed zone near a truck weigh station
A highway lane restricted to trucks
questions.exp: The No Zone describes the four areas around a large truck where the driver's visibility is severely limited: directly in front (~20 feet), behind (~200 feet), and on both sides. Avoid staying in any No Zone.

questions.q: Which of the following best reduces the chance of a crash at night?
opts: Driving faster to spend less time on the road
Using high beams at all times for maximum visibility
Slowing down, maximizing alertness, and keeping headlights clean and properly aimed
Following other vehicles closely to use their lights
questions.exp: Night driving requires greater caution. Reduce speed so you can stop within your headlight range. Keep headlights clean and aimed correctly. Avoid looking directly at oncoming headlights.

questions.q: If you experience a sudden steering loss (tire failure or loss of power steering), you should:
opts: Brake hard and steer sharply to the shoulder
Keep both hands on the wheel, maintain your direction, ease off the gas, and allow the vehicle to slow before carefully steering to safety
Immediately stop in your lane and turn on hazard lights
Shift to a lower gear and apply the parking brake
questions.exp: Maintain a two-hand grip and keep the vehicle pointed forward. Sudden steering or braking can cause loss of control. Allow the vehicle to slow naturally, then ease toward the shoulder.

questions.q: When approaching an intersection where a traffic light has just turned green, you should:
opts: Accelerate immediately through the intersection
Check that cross traffic has actually stopped before proceeding
Blast your horn to warn any red-light runners
Wait for the vehicle behind you to urge you forward
questions.exp: A 'fresh green' is one of the most dangerous traffic light situations. Red-light runners may still be in the intersection. Pause briefly and verify cross traffic has stopped before you enter.

questions.q: The most common contributing factor in highway crashes is:
opts: Poor road design
Mechanical failure
Driver inattention, distraction, or fatigue
Bad weather
questions.exp: Studies consistently show that driver error — primarily inattention, distraction, and fatigue — is the most frequent factor in crashes. Conditions like weather are contributing factors, not primary causes.

questions.q: When driving in very heavy rain, what is the greatest tire-related hazard?
opts: Tire blowouts from wet road debris
Hydroplaning — tires riding on a film of water and losing traction
Increased tire pressure from heat and rain
Sidewall damage from puddles
questions.exp: Hydroplaning is the primary tire hazard in heavy rain. It can occur at speeds as low as 35 mph on wet roads. Properly inflated tires with adequate tread significantly reduce the risk.

questions.q: When merging onto a highway, if there is not a safe gap in traffic, you should:
opts: Force your way in — highway traffic must yield to merging vehicles
Stop at the end of the ramp and wait
Slow or stop in the merge lane and wait for a safe gap before entering
Sound your horn to alert traffic to make room
questions.exp: Merging vehicles must yield to highway traffic. If no safe gap exists, slow at the end of the merge lane (or briefly stop) and wait for one. Never stop on the highway itself if you can avoid it.

questions.q: One early warning sign that you may be becoming drowsy while driving is:
opts: Driving slightly faster than usual
Missing exits or turn-offs, lane drifting, or frequent blinking
Feeling hungry
The radio seems louder than normal
questions.exp: Missing exits, drifting from your lane, heavy eyelids, and difficulty remembering the last few miles are all signs of drowsiness. Pull over immediately and rest.

questions.q: The purpose of rumble strips on the highway shoulder is to:
opts: Mark the lane boundaries for bicycles
Alert drowsy or distracted drivers who drift off the road through sound and vibration
Provide traction for vehicles on the edge of the road
Mark no-parking zones along the shoulder
questions.exp: Rumble strips are grooved patterns pressed into the road surface at the lane edge or shoulder. The vibration and noise they create serve as a sensory alarm for drivers who have drifted from their lane.

questions.q: ABS (Anti-lock Braking System) is designed to:
opts: Stop the vehicle in the shortest possible distance on all surfaces
Automatically steer the vehicle around obstacles
Prevent wheel lockup during hard braking so the driver can maintain steering control
Reduce fuel consumption during deceleration
questions.exp: ABS rapidly pulses braking pressure many times per second to prevent wheel lockup. This keeps the tires rolling and allows you to steer while applying maximum braking force.

questions.q: If you must drive through a flooded road (and the water depth is shallow), the safest approach is to:
opts: Speed through to minimize the time in water
Drive through slowly and steadily in low gear; test brakes immediately after
Shift to neutral and coast through
Drive through at normal speed and pump the brakes continuously
questions.exp: If you must cross a shallow flooded section, go slowly in a low gear to maintain momentum without causing engine damage. Immediately afterward, gently tap the brakes several times to dry them.

questions.q: The best overall strategy for avoiding crashes on any road in any condition is:
opts: Driving at the exact speed limit
Keeping your vehicle well maintained
Maintaining a space cushion, eliminating distractions, staying alert, and actively scanning far ahead
Never driving faster than 45 mph
questions.exp: There is no single strategy — safe driving requires combining good habits: active scanning, space cushion, zero distractions, appropriate speed, and consistent alertness. These habits prevent the vast majority of crashes.
